It was actually spoken by her political ally, Sir Keith Joseph.",
  "speaker": "Sir Keith Joseph",
  "date": "19 October 1974",
  "source_event": "Speech in Edgbaston, Birmingham",
  "stable_locator": "Margaret Thatcher Foundation, Document 101830",
  "historical_context": "Sir Keith Joseph delivered this highly controversial speech in Edgbaston shortly after the October 1974 general election, addressing the moral state of Britain and criticizing socialist intellectuals.",
  "immediate_subject": "The perceived anti-nationalism of left-wing intellectuals.",
  "intended_argument": "That socialist intellectuals are driven by a disdain for their own country and countrymen, contrasting with true patriotism.",
  "literal_meaning": "George Orwell noted that left-wing intellectuals hate their own country and fellow Englishmen despite preaching universal brotherhood.",
  "broader_principle": "Abstract internationalism and professed love for humanity often mask a deep-seated resentment toward one's own nation and culture.",
  "mechanism": "By invoking George Orwell, a respected socialist, Joseph validates his critique of the modern left's lack of patriotism.",
  "claimed_consequence": "The denigration of patriotism by intellectuals weakens the national will and societal cohesion.",
  "entities": [
    "George Orwell",
    "Sir Keith Joseph",
    "Edgbaston",
    "Birmingham",
    "Conservative Party"
  ],
  "editorial_guidance": {
    "desired_first_impression": "A stark critique of left-wing intellectualism delivered by a key architect of Thatcherism.",

      "Attribute to Sir Keith Joseph, not Margaret Thatcher.",
      "Contextualize within the 1974 Edgbaston speech."
